bib.title: Natural Language Processing with Python, Chapter 2: Accessing Text Corpora and Lexical Resources

question: What text corpora and lexical resources are available in NLTK, and how are they accessed and combined with Python?
contributions: Tour of NLTK corpus readers (Gutenberg, Brown, Reuters, Inaugural, UDHR, NPS Chat) and their structures
ConditionalFreqDist as the tool for per-category counts
Lexical resources: wordlists, stopwords, names, CMU pronouncing dictionary, Swadesh, Toolbox, WordNet
WordNet hierarchy, lexical relations and path-based similarity

limits: Written for Python 2 and NLTK 2.x (2009); most code in the chapter does not run unchanged on Python 3 / NLTK 3.
Dated API: print statements (print word,), no parentheses; Python 2 integer division needs from __future__ import division.

Dated API: WordNet attributes were properties in NLTK 2 (synset.lemma_names, .definition, .examples, .lemmas, lemma.name, synset.name, lemma.synset); in NLTK 3 they are methods (lemma_names(), definition(), examples(), lemmas(), name(), synset()).
Dated API: nltk.bigrams(sent) returned a list; in NLTK 3 it returns a generator.
Dated API: cfd.tabulate/plot and FreqDist behave differently in NLTK 3 (FreqDist subclasses Counter; iteration order is no longer sorted by frequency; cfd[condition].max() is now most_common(1)).
Dated API: the Inaugural cfd example prints 'file[:4]' in one listing and 'fileid[:4]' in the other; the first is a typo and fails.
Dated API: dict key order and list(cfd['romance']) frequency ordering shown in output depend on NLTK 2 / Python 2.
Dated API: nltk.app.wordnet() GUI browser and the 'from book import *' idiom were replaced by nltk.download() and from nltk.book import *.
Dated: wordnet data is WordNet 3.0 here; modern installs need nltk.download('wordnet') and wordnet corpora also need 'omw-1.4' for some APIs.
Dated: stopword list shown is the 2,400-entry list (Table 2-2) but nltk.corpus.stopwords.words('english') in current NLTK is a ~180-word list, so the content fraction 0.66 would not reproduce.
Counts are raw and not normalized by genre size; no significance testing; WordNet counts 155,287 words / 117,659 synsets conflict with Table 2-2's 145k.
Table 2-2 and the corpora of the era (Brown, Reuters ModApte-style split) are small by modern standards; WordNet similarity scores are described by the authors as numbers that 'won't mean much'.
The page watermark from the download site was ignored and is not quoted.
practices: Use corpus reader methods fileids(), categories(), raw(), words(), sents() for uniform access (Table 2-3, Sec 2.1).
Use a ConditionalFreqDist built from (condition, event) pairs to compare word usage across genres, time or languages (Sec 2.2).
Filter stopwords before further processing because they have little lexical content and do not distinguish texts (Sec 2.4).
Use a wordlist to find unusual or misspelled words by set difference against the text vocabulary (Example 2-3).
Navigate WordNet by synset, lemma, hypernym, hyponym, meronym and holonym relations (Sec 2.5).
Use lowest_common_hypernyms and min_depth to judge how close two synsets are; deeper shared ancestors imply closer meanings (Sec 2.5).
Use path_similarity as a 0-1 score (-1 if no path) for semantic relatedness, e.g. to match a search for vehicle to documents with limousine (Sec 2.5).
Put reusable code in functions and modules rather than retyping; do not name a file nltk.py (Sec 2.3).
Greedy next-word choice with max() loops; choose randomly among likely words instead (Example 2-1).

terms.definition: a text corpus is a large body of text
A conditional frequency distribution is a collection of frequency distributions, each one for a different 'condition.'
A lexicon, or lexical resource, is a collection of words and/or phrases along with associated information, such as part-of-speech and sense definitions.
A lexical entry consists of a headword (also known as a lemma) along with additional information, such as the part-of-speech and the sense definition.
Two distinct words having the same spelling are called homonyms.
phonetic codes, distinct labels for each contrastive sound
This pairing of a synset with a word is called a lemma.
edges indicate the hypernym/hyponym relation, i.e., the relation between superordinate and subordinate concepts
Some concepts are very general, such as Entity, State, Event; these are called unique beginners or root synsets.
items to their components (meronyms) or to the things they are contained in (holonyms)
the act of walking involves the act of stepping, so walking entails stepping
The polysemy of a word is the number of senses it has.
the frequency of a word type is inversely proportional to its rank (i.e., f x r = k, for some constant k)
